Memberships purchased in the reporting month

The one-line version, if you read nothing else.

127 classes sit unspent on memberships the studio has already been paid for — about ₹12,74,275 of value sitting in members’ hands. The people who have used a quarter or less of what they bought are the most winnable names on the file and the least contacted.

The membership ledger for Supreme HQ, Bandra holds 325 rows covering 245 people. 121 of them were paid for, carrying ₹13,96,809 of recorded money. 1% of that money belongs to memberships now marked lapsed.

This chapter is written for September 2026 at Supreme HQ, Bandra: the first sections date the churn to that month alone — what was bought, what closed, and what runs out next. The rest reads the selected-month membership-purchase cohort as a funnel: what a membership is worth when it is bought, how long it lasts, how much of it is used, and how it ends — the context the month’s numbers need to be judged against.

The median paid membership at this studio lasts 8 days. Not months. And the way it ends is not a single story: 64 memberships recorded no attendance at all, while the rest ran down their classes and stopped. Those are different failures, they cost different things to fix, and the studio currently treats them as one number called churn.

September 2026, dated

Churn that actually happened in the selected month

The ledger dates every membership, so September 2026 can be read on its own with event dates scoped to the reporting month. During September 2026, 164 memberships were recorded as churned at Supreme HQ, Bandra — ₹4,61,481 of paid money closing out, and 16 of them had never produced a single attendance.

On the other side of the same month, 121 paid memberships were bought for ₹13,96,809. Those two numbers together are the net movement of the book in September 2026. The following sections describe the selected-month purchase cohort, because the month’s churn can only be judged against what this studio usually loses.

298 memberships (249 people) run out within thirty days after September 2026, carrying ₹24,21,521 of paid value. That is next month’s churn list, already known and already contactable.

The churn of September 2026 was not mostly burnt-out loyalists: those closed memberships had used 68% of their classes on average, and the table below shows the largest of them.

The shape of the churn book

How a membership ends, and when

The book, by the state the system holds it in: Renewal Grace Period 202 · Not Activated 46 · Active 25 · Renewed 24 · Lapsed 17 · New 11.

81% of the ledger is live or in a grace window. Everything else is finished. A studio that reads only its live book sees a healthy club and a small one; the whole file says the club has met, and lost, 63 people.

Survival falls fastest at the start and never really stops: 52% of paid memberships are still running after Day 7s, 0% after thirty days, and 0.0% after a year. The shape says the problem is in the first month, where nothing is charged and nothing is measured.

The two ways to lose a member

One never started. One finished.
64 memberships recorded no attendance at all, 20% of the ledger. 17 of them were paid for. These people bought a promise and never used it; the studio has their money and their goodwill, and it is losing both quietly.

The other failure is the opposite: a member who came, used the product, and finished it. Those memberships are not churn in any meaningful sense — they are short products selling short. The distinction decides whether the fix is an activation programme or a pricing change, and today it is not made anywhere in the reporting.

Usage tells the difference cleanly: nothing used 101 · up to a quarter 9 · a quarter to a half 4 · a half to three quarters 3 · three quarters to all 4. The members who used nothing have a median membership of 14 days; those who used everything ran 22 days. One group left; the other finished.

Did they use what they paid for?

The classes the studio owes and nobody is claiming

22 paid memberships have a usage figure recorded. Of them, 11 used a quarter or less of what they bought, leaving 127 classes undelivered, and 4 used everything.

Undelivered classes are the studio’s cheapest retention tool and its largest unmanaged liability. They are worth real money to the member, they cost nothing to grant as visits, and every one of them represents a member who has already decided to come and has not come.

The decline that comes first

What the visit pattern says weeks before the status changes

Churn shows up in the visit pattern long before it shows up in the status. Comparing each membership’s first half against its second, across 33 memberships with more than three visits to split: 85% came less often in the second half, 64% by at least half, and only 9% came more often. The median run fell from 7 visits to 1.

That is the leading indicator the studio is missing. Attendance decline is visible weeks before a membership lapses, it is computable from data the studio already exports, and it identifies people who can still be reached — unlike lapsed members, whom the file says are gone.

Product by product

Which membership churns, and which merely ends

Product by product, the churn is not evenly spread: Extended 10 Single Class Pack ₹2,27,272 · 12 Class Package ₹2,23,453 · 1 Month Unlimited Membership ₹2,13,519 · Single Class ₹71,872 · Newcomers 2 For 1 ₹48,562.

The largest seller is Extended 10 Single Class Pack (13 sold, ₹2,27,272), which runs 90 days at a mean usage of ·%, and is still live on 100% of them. The products that hold best are not the ones that sell most, and that gap is the studio’s product question: the file is being steered by a number nobody chose on purpose.

0% of the money in these products sits on memberships that are live fewer than one time in ten. That is the pool the studio re-sells to every month, at full acquisition cost, and it is a product decision rather than a marketing one.

Who is winnable

Recency, unspent value, and the ones who asked to pause

By recency rather than by value, the winnable book looks like this: attended in the last 30 days 81 people holding ₹10,33,461 · 31 to 60 days ago 12 people holding ₹21,368 · over 180 days ago 15 people holding ₹2,19,446.

93 people have been in the building within the last sixty days and still hold ₹10,54,829 of undelivered value. They are not a win-back campaign; they are an existing member with an unspent credit, and the difference in contact cost between the two is the entire difference in outcome.

A separate signal the studio is not using: 10 memberships were frozen at some point (3.1% of the ledger), and those are live more often than the ones that were not — 100.0% against 76.5%. A member who asks to pause is not leaving; they are the one who intends to come back and wants the clock stopped.

What the lost book cost

Churn, priced

The lost book is not an abstraction. ₹9,712 of recorded membership money has been paid for and finished — 1% of everything the studio has ever booked on this ledger. With an average ticket of ₹11,544 and a median life of 8 days, that ticket has to be re-earned every 8 days per member.

Put beside what a sale costs to win — the studio collected ₹11,003 per buyer in september — churn stops being a marketing problem and becomes the reason the marketing budget exists.

Discounting at the point of sale does not buy durability here: none is live 77% of the time. Discount and churn are close to independent in this file, which is its own finding — the studio can stop buying retention with price and start buying it with programming.

What else could explain it

Causes the studio has not considered

Churn is the chapter where the obvious explanation is usually wrong, so each candidate is stated with what would have to be true.

Supported

The product is short, not the member disloyal

The median paid membership runs 8 days and the modal product is a one-month or small-pack purchase. A short product that is fully used is not churn.

Split the churn number by whether usage exceeded 90% before deciding what to fix.
Supported

Nobody is onboarded

64 memberships never produced a single attendance, and 17 of those were paid for.

An activation contact in the first fourteen days is the whole intervention.
Partly

Price and discount

Discount taken at purchase shows no consistent relationship with how long a membership lives in this file.

Do not conclude discounts cause churn; conclude they do not prevent it, which is a different decision.
Ruled out

The competition took them

The exports contain no competitor or cancellation-reason field. Anything said about why members went to another studio is a hypothesis, not a finding.

Ask directly, on the day the status changes, and record the answer in the same file.

Method and limitations

How to read these numbers, and what they cannot show
Evidence — what was read, and how much of it belongs to this studio
FileSourceRows in fileRows for this studioDate span
Day End Report - Part 1 - New (9).csvnewmembers21,17121,171

Sales - Raw - Sales (23).csvsales25,04425,044
❖ PM - Leads ❖ - ◉ Leads (31).csvleads25,31525,315
Every figure in this chapter is computed from these rows. Nothing is estimated, extrapolated or carried over from another month.

Definitions used in this chapter

  • Membership. one row of the lapsed and new-members export, filtered to purchases in the selected reporting month. Status and usage attributes reflect the uploaded export.
  • Paid. a membership whose amount paid is above zero and whose name is not a staff, complimentary, credit or referral product.
  • Lapsed. the Derived Status column as the system computes it, cross-checked against the churn and end dates on the row.
  • Lifetime. end date minus purchase date, or, for memberships still open, today minus purchase date. Open memberships are therefore treated as censored, not as survivors.
  • Usage. the Sessions Used % column, which the studio records against the classes granted, not the money paid.

The ledger starts wherever the export starts. Memberships that were created and deleted before the file’s first day are not in it, so very early churn may be understated.

No cancellation reason is recorded anywhere in these files. The reports say what happened to a membership, never why the member says it happened.

Money shown is what the studio recorded as paid for the membership, not revenue recognised; unused classes are still a liability rather than income.

A member may hold several memberships at once. Counts of memberships and counts of people are deliberately kept apart in every table.

Recommendations

14 actions, ordered by the size of the value each releases
01

Write the unspent classes back as visits, with a date on them

Front Desk + Finance

Reasoning11 memberships used a quarter or less of what they bought, leaving 127 classes undelivered worth about ₹12,53,970.

Expected impactConverting credit into booked attendance moves money the studio already holds onto the balance sheet and pulls the member back into a routine - the single cheapest retention action available.

02

Segment win-back by recency, not by lifetime value

CRM + Marketing

Reasoning81 people were here in the last thirty days and still hold ₹10,33,461; the largest group, 15 people, has not been inside a year.

Expected impactContact cost per recovered member falls by an order of magnitude between those two groups, and the studio currently sends the same message to both.

03

Freeze, do not lose: treat a pause request as a save

Front Desk

Reasoning10 memberships were frozen at some point and 100.0% are still live, against 76.5% of those that were never frozen.

Expected impactA member who asks to pause is planning to return. Offering the pause before they offer the cancellation converts a churn event into a deferred one.

04

Put every member on a plan at the halfway point of their membership

Studio Manager

Reasoning85% of measurable memberships attended less in their second half than their first, and 64% attended at least half as often. The change is visible before the status moves.

Expected impactA mid-membership review - attendance so far, what is left, one specific class to book - is the only intervention in this chapter that can act before the lapse rather than after it.

05

Run an activation sequence through the first fortnight

Front Desk + CRM

Reasoning79% of paid memberships end within fourteen days and 100% within thirty.

Expected impactThe first two weeks decide the membership. A dated plan, a booked class and a call on day ten is the whole intervention.

06

Collect the unused classes

CRM + Front Desk

Reasoning11 memberships used a quarter or less of what they bought, leaving 127 classes unspent.

Expected impactPaid-for and undelivered is a liability and a warm reason to make contact.

07

Lead with the product that keeps its members

Sales + Marketing

ReasoningSingle Class is still live or renewed 84% of the time, the best rate in the range.

Expected impactRenewal is a property of the product list before it is a property of the customer. What works should be sold first.

08

Put the churn number in the acquisition plan

Management + Finance

ReasoningMedian membership life is 8 days.

Expected impactIf most of the book has to be replaced each month, acquisition is a maintenance cost rather than a growth line, and it should be budgeted as one.

09

Make the mid-length products the default recommendation

Sales + Marketing

ReasoningMemberships of 31 to 60 days carry ₹17,570 of average cash against ₹1,942 for a week-long product.

Expected impactThe short products are the ones that leave. What a member buys first predicts how long they stay far better than how much they liked the trial.

10

Convert the single-class buyers before the week is out

Front Desk + CRM

Reasoning36 memberships lasted a week or less and used 0.92 classes each.

Expected impactThis is the largest, cheapest and most time-sensitive group in the ledger. A call on day three is worth more than any win-back offer in month three.

11

Work the not-activated and grace-period files monthly

CRM + Front Desk

Reasoning46 memberships never activated and 202 sit inside the grace window.

Expected impactBoth are dated, small and contactable. A monthly standing list keeps this number from building up into a churn statistic.

12

Offer the unspent classes back as visits, not as credit

CRM

Reasoning11 memberships used a quarter or less of what they paid for, leaving 127 classes unspent.

Expected impactUndelivered classes are already paid for. Converting them into visits rebuilds the habit; converting them into credit only postpones the decision to leave.

13

Price a three-month product deliberately

Sales + Management

ReasoningThe median membership life is 8 days.

Expected impactIf the median life is inside the second month, a three-month product sets a different expectation and gives the studio two renewal conversations instead of one.

14

Read churn by joining month, not only by product

CRM

Reasoning325 memberships sit in the ledger, 121 of them paid.

Expected impactMembers who joined in the same month behave similarly. Cohort lines show whether retention is improving or whether the mix is merely changing.
